FOREWORD
Users of various civil engineering codes have been feeling the need for explanatory handbooks and other compilations based on Indian Standards. The need has been further emphasized in view of the publication of the National Building Code of India in 1970 and its implementation. The Expert Group set up in 1972 by the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India carried out in-depth studies in various areas of civil engineering and construction practices. During the preparation of the Fifth Five Year Plan in 1975, the Group was assigned the task of producing a Science and Technology plan for research, development and extension work in the sector of housing and construction technology. One of the items of this plan was the production of design handbooks, explanatory handbooks and design aids based on the National Building Code and various Indian Standards, and other activities in the promotion of the National Building Code. The Expert Group gave high priority to this item and on the recommendation of the Department of Science and Technology the Planning Commission approved the following two projects which were assigned to the Indian Standards Institution: a) Development programme on Code civil engineering construction, and b) Typification for industrial buildings. implementation for building and

A Special Committee for Implementation of Science andTechnology Projects ( SCIP ) consisting of experts connected with different aspects was set up in 1974 to advise the ISI Directorate General in identifying the Handbook and for guiding the development of the work. Under the first project, the Committee has so far identified subjects for several explanatory handbooks/compilations covering appropriate Indian Standards/Codes/Specifications which include the following: Design Aids for Reinforced Handbook Concrete to IS : 456-1978 ( SP : 16-1980 ) ( IS : 1893) Explanatory on Masonry Code ( SP : 20-1981

Explanatory Handbook on Codes of Earthquake 1975 and IS : 4326-1976 ) ( SP : 22-1982 ) Handbook on Concrete Mixes ( SP : 23-1982 )

One of the handbooks suggested is the Functional Requirements of Industrial Buildings. This Handbook covers the requirements relating to lighting and ventilation. The handbook is expected to provide explanation regarding various provisions given in Indian Standard relating to lighting and ventilation for industrial buildings. This also gives typical worked out examples, design aids and charts to enable the designer to use them directly in the design according to the existing code and recommendations. The Handbook, it is hoped, would provide useful guidance to architects, engineers and other agencies dealing with lighting, ventilation and illuminating engineering aspects of industrial buildings. The Handbook is based on the draft prepared by Shri B. J. Ramrakhiani, Directorate General of Factory Advice Retired Deputy Director General, Service and Labour Institute, Ministry of Labour (Government of India). The draft Handbook was reviewed by Shri S. Roy Choudhary, Peico Electronics & Electricals, Bombay; Shri M. S. Lulla, Engnieering Consultant, Madras; Shri L. G. Bartake, S. F. India Limited, Bombay and Dr B. K. Saxena, Central Building Research Institute, Roorkee who had offered valuable comments, and their views have been taken into consideration, while finalizing the Handbook.

SECTION 1

LIGHTING

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 Good lighting enables workers in factory buildings to carry out their visual tasks easily, quickly and without fatigue and to move about in work areas safely. It also helps in cutting down wastage and rejects, in utilising floor space efficiently and in boosting morale and thus in improving the overall performance of the factory.
1.2 The Factories Act provides that sufficient and suitable lighting either natural or artificial or both shall be provided and maintained in every part of the factory where workers are working or passing. Therefore, while speaking of good lighting, we are talking of lighting to be not only sufficient, that is, the quantity of illumination required at the workplaces and approaches, but also suitable, that is the quality of lighting, and this brings in concepts like glare, uniformity of distribution, brightness contrast, direction of lighting, and colour and colour rendering. These concepts will be discussed later ( see 3 ). First of all, we will consider what is meant by the lighting to be sufficient, that is, the quantity of light. 2. ILLUMINATION LEVELS

and these include many jobs in various industrial buildings and processes. The levels of illumination for various industrial buildings and processes recommended in the Indian Standard are given in Table 1. These are based on visibility parameters, that is, size of the task, brightness, brightness contrast and visual capacity in terms of time required to see the task, and have been adopted from the values developed by the Illumination Engineering Society of the USA. These values are valid under most of the conditions, whether the illumination is by daylighting, artificial lighting or a combination of the two. 2.2 The values of illumination given below are based on difficulty of seeing the various tasks in factories and offices: a) Most difficult seeing tasks, such as extra fine assembly; precision grading, extra-fine finishing 10 000 lux

b)

Very difficult seeing tasks, such as fine assembly, high speed work, fine finishing and critical seeing tasks, such as ordinary bench work and assembly, machine shop work, finishing of medium and fine parts, office work Ordinary seeing tasks, such as automatic machine operations, rough grading, continuous processes, packing, and shipping seeing tasks, such as stair-ways, wash rooms and other surface areas, active storages Rough seeing tasks, such as corridors, passages, inactive storages

1 000 lux

2.1 Task Illumination - The quantity of light at a workplace depends upon the visual task so that the individual worker can see the task clearly, accurately and without eye strain. If the size of the critical detail of any visual task and its reflection characterstic are known, it is possible to state the appropriate value of illumination in lux ( defined as lumens of flux per ms of the surface of the task ), which will enable the visual task to be performed satisfactorily. Good lighting, however, requires the consideration of safety and welfare along with that of visual efficiency. The levels of illumination recommended are, therefore, based on visual performance and amenity. These values of illumination levels for various tasks and locations are given in IS : 3646 ( Part 2 ) - 1966* *Code of practice for interior illumination, Part 2 Schedule for values of illumination and glare index.

that the illumination of rooms which open off a working area should be fairly high even though the rooms may be used only occasionally. Similarly, entrances to the factory should receive adequate levels of building illumination both during day and night so that workers entering or leaving the building can do so without risk of accidents. During day, windows may be provided to allow adequate natural lighting at the immediate entrance, grading to lower levels further inside the entrance area; and at night, the illumination levels should reduce towards the exits and no bright fittings should be placed in the line of sight of people leaving the building. 3. CHARACTERISTICS

150

OF GOOD LIGH-

TING

150 200

3.1 The following characteristics with regard to the quality are to be given due consideration for planning the lighting for the task or tasks in view.
3.1.1 Glare - Glare is caused due to an uneven distribution of light sources or due to excessive contrast or abrupt changes in brightness in space and time or by seeing light sources or sun directly or after reflection from polished surfaces. An example of glare source in daylighting is the view of the bright sky through a window or a skylight specially when the surrounding wall or ceiling is dark or weakly illuminated. This kind of direct glare can be minimised either by shielding the open sky from direct sight by means of louvers, external hoods or deep reveals or by cross-lighting the surrounding to a comparable level. Other direct sources of glare can be screened by providing either louvers or reflectors. Local lighting at the work bench or machines should have opaque reflectors. Indirect glare can be avoided by carefully positioning the light sauces in relation to glare surfaces and line of vision or by painting objects in matte. 3.1.2 Uniformi~ of Distribution - It is usually desirable to provide reasonably uniform general illumination over the entire work area. A gradual transition of brightness with diversity ratio of not less than O-7 from one area to the other within the field of vision not only ensures reasonable uniformity but also minimises glare. Maximum and minimum illumination at any point should not be more than one-sixth above or below the average level in the area. Maximum spacing to mounting height ratios are generally specified for different types of luminaires for attaining reasonable uniformity ( see 6.6 ) . In daylighting design also, the uniformity of illumination distribution over the work area could be achieved by suitable positioning of windows and glazings and by increasing the internal reflected component of daylight factor (see 4 ). However, the uniformity of workplace

300

2.3 Where visual task is required to be carried on throughout an interior of the factory building, general level of illumination of the value recommended is necessary. This value of illumination is required to be provided on a horizontal working plane at the level of 85 cm above the floor level, unless the precise height and location of the task is known or specified, in wh"lch case the level of illumination required is on the task itself. Where the task is localised or different tasks are carried on inside the same building, the recommended value is for the task or tasks only. For reasons of economy, it need not, and sometimes should not, be the general level of illumination used throughout the factory building and the judicious combination of supplementary lighting and local lighting is required to be provided to suit the various tasks, Some industrial processes call for lighting of a particular quality, in which case, as mentioned above, the level of illumination is only one of the factors to be taken into account.

illumination is not so critical in the daylighting design as in the artificial lighting. 3.1.3 Brightness Contrast - The brightness of an object depends upon the amount of light flux incident and proportion of that light reflected or transmitted in the direction of the eye. Proper brightness ratio or brightness contrast between adjacent surfaces is an important requirement of good lighting. Excessive brightness ratios, even though not severe enough to cause glare, may be seriously detrimental to lighting quality. Generally the task should be brighter than both the immediate background and general surroundings; as an example, workplace should be brighter than the working table and floor area. Where the illumination levels are above 300 lux, the ratio of average brightness between the task, immediate backmay be and general surroundings ground 10:3:1. Since the illumination for the task and the immediate background are usually much the same, desirable ratio could be achieved by choosing a finish for the background having lower reflection factor. The following brightness ratios are recommended for industrial areas: Ratio, 3 : 1 10 : 1 20 : 1 40 : 1 Location Between task background. and immediate of the object, provided the brightness and the brightness contrast remain the same. However, there are psychological effects of colour in lighting, namely, the feeling of coolness, depression and distance for green and blue colours, and the feeling of warmth, stimulation and nearness for red, orange any yellow colours. 3.1.5.2 The appearance of coloured surfaces depends on their spectral reflection characteristics and the spectral composition of the light illuminating them, and is therefore different for light sources of different spectral composition. This property of light sources is known as colour rendering. This quality is made use of for such specialised jobs where critical colour judgements or comparisons are of importance, such as cotton grading, colour matching of paints and certain inspection tasks. For such jobs, specially designed lighting systems are preferred to natural lighting and the lamps are selected on the basis of their colour rendering properties rather than luminous efficiency. In some applications, the advantage can also be taken of the colour distortion produced by a light source for enhancing the contrast between the different parts of the task. That is why mercury vapour lamps are generally used in coal picking belts in collieries. 3.1.6 Strosboscoflic E$ect and nicker from Discharge Lamps - When discharge lamps are operating on alternating current, their light output varies with each cycle and this produces certain effects known as flicker. It can cause annoyance. Flickering also occurs due to half-way rectification in fluorescent tubular lamps and causes strosboscopic effect whereby rotating machinery or other objects appear to slow down in speed and this may lead to accidents. The combination of light from lamps on two electrical circuits, one lagging and the other leading in phase, reduces the effects arising out of cyclic variation of light output. Similarly, strosboscopic effect can be eliminated in fluorescent fittings by employing special circuits, and in the case of high pressure mercury vapour ( HPMV ) lamps, by installing lamps on three-phase power system so that the light emitted by the lamps overlaps. The flicker in fluorescent lamps is most noticeable at the ends and these should be shielded from the direct view. 3.1.7 Colour Dynamics

3.1.4 Direction of Lighting and Dz@usion - The light gest diffused when it flows from various random directions. It is measured in terms of the absence of sharp shadows. The degree of diffusion desirable for a task depends upon the type of work to be performed. For instance, for preventing specular reflections, such as in viewing polished metal surface in a machine shop, a highly diffused light is essential. The appearance of a three-dimensional object on the other hand is affected by the directional use of component of light. By appropriate directional lighting and control of the size and positioning of the light sources, solid shape of the component parts of some tasks and details of surface texture or polish can be enhance,d or suppressed - a facility particularly of importance in the lighting of many inspection processes. 3.1.5 Cotour and Colour Rendering

3.1.7.1 As has already been pointed out, the eye sees an object by the light it reflects and distinguishes its details chiefly by colour contrasts. A good white paint reflects 80 percent or more of the light; a good black paint reflects only a small percentage of light; a dirty grim-faced wall in a factory may absorb 90 percent or even more of the light it receives; dark dirty machinery may be nearly as bad. If

SP : 32 - 1966 the place is cleaned-up and the walls are painted or colour washed with pleasing light tone having moderate reflecting qualities and the machine parts are painted to given a moderate contrast with walls and the work, the viewing of tasks can be greatly improved without Only when increasing the light intensity. clean-up and painting is done, can it be determined whether any further benefit could be derived by increasing the illumination level. 3.1.7.2 Since the white paintsare distracting and do not afford much contrast, the walls should not be painted white. The ceilings can be white or nearly so when they are out of line of vision. The machine parts that constitute the background for the task should also be of soft hue without high reflection qualities. In determining the choice, the colour of the material being worked should be taken into account. For key parts of machines, such as guards or control levers, a colour that stands out should be chosen. Yellow orange or yellow green has maximum visibility ranking even higher than the conventional red in this respect. But early developers of fluorescent light drew on scientific findings that the human eye is most sensitive to yellow-green light and designed their lamp to most strongly to those colours the standard ccool white' fluorescent light in use today. 3.1.8.3 One of the steps to minimize the biological hazards of fluorescent lighting in factories and other places of work is to use broad-spectrum lamp instead of the narrowspectrum `cool white' lamps in common use. Light stress could be reduced by mixing fluorescent and incandescent light in workplace, and wherever possible, by providing skylight and windows to bring in sunlight 4. DAYLIGHTING 4.1 As a rule, daylighting is preferable to artificial lighting as it is a potential natural source of light which meets all the requirements of good lighting. Therefore, when a factory is to be built, the shape of the building is usually planned on the basis of daylighting. It is only very rarely that factory space will be planned with a view to obtaining the most favourable artificial lighting. Except in factories having multiple shifts, the buildings will be used during more hours per day by natural lighting than by artificial illumination. One may, therefore, safely base the layout of the factory buildings on natural daylighting, because artificial lighting can be easily manipulated to suit the different circumstances. 4.2 The prime source of light for daylighting is the sun. The availability of daylight outdoor in the plains in this country is quite high throughout the year. The light received by the earth from the sun consists of two parts, namely, direct solar illumination ( direct sunlight being excluded ) and sky radiation. The latter is nearly constant through the major portion of the day, while the sunlight ( direct solar illumination ) can be as much as four times the skylight. The wide variation and the chances that incidence of direct sunlight over moving machinery in factory floors during certain hours of the day can cause undesirable visual fatigue and may become a source of danger, necessitates its exclusion in the planning of apertures for daylighting. Therefore, for the purpose of daylighting design direct solar illumination is not considered and only sky radiation is taken as contributing to the illumination of the factory interiors during the day. 5. Artzjkial Light and Health

3.1.8.1 Recent studies have shown that long hours of the day and night under artificial light causes many biological and other health problems. Excessive exposure to ultra-violet radiation can cause skin cancer. Unshielded fluorescent lights may be increasing by five percent the weekly dose of ultra violet radiation, many office and factory workers are receiving. For sensitive persons, added dose could already be causing cancer. Even more disturbing factor is that the potent unnatural wavelengths of fluorescent light can cause genetic mutation, cancer and death in the cells of many living things, including man, at a significantly high rate. 3.1.8.2 As is already known, fluorescent lamp gives off or `fluorescences' when a coating of phosphors inside the tube is hit by ultra*Paint machinery and equipment in light colours with matte finish. 11

The luminance ( brightness ) distribution of such a sky is non-uniform; the horizoe is brighter than the zenith and brightness distribution in the region away from the sun varying as cosecant of the angle of view between 15" and 90' above horizon and remaining constant between 0" and 15" above horizon. 5.1.2 The clear design sky basis holds good for any orientation of the building and ensures adequate daylighting indoors for about 90 per cent of the day-time working hours. The correillumination on a sponding exterior design horizontal plane for the clear design sky is taken as 8 000 lux from the entire sky vault, direct sunlight being excluded and that due to the sky and the sun as 16 000 lux. In between the morning and evening solar altitude of 15", the indoor illumination increases as the sun goes up in the sky. 5.1.1 The Central Building Research Institute, Roorkee ( UP ) has developed a concept of clear design sky as the basis of daylighting design in this country and this has been adopted by the Indian Standards Institution in their

SP : 32 - 1986 to be nearly constant all over the country. the prevalent atmospheric haze However, which varies from place to place may necessitate a 25 percent increase in the value of 8 000 lux design illumination where haze conditions prevail at design time. 5.2 Daylight Factor Since the brightness of the sky is constantly changing, it follows that the light inside a building must change, and therefore, it is not practical to estimate the .efhciency of a system of fenestration of a building in absolute units such as lux. The visual appreciation of the increase in the magnitude of the light is damped by overall increase in adaptation level, and the ultimate criterion of efficient illumination is its effect on the observer. In a building the eye of the observer automatically tends to make a comparison with the brightness in his working environment and the brightness of the part of the sky visible through the windows or skylights; in other words, he judges good daylighting less by a sense of actual intensity than by one of proportion. Therefore, daylight at a point indoors is usually measured, as in fact appraised, as a ratio of the total illumination which would be received at the same moment out-of-doors from an unobstructed view of the clear design sky ( excluding direct sunlight ). This ratio is called daylight factor, and is expressed as a percentage. Thus, the daylight factor of 1 percent at a point inside a building would signify the illumination of 1 percent of that which would be obtained if the whole of the hemisphere of the sky were contributing light. Since exterior design illumination for clear design sky is taken as 8 000 Iux, the daylight factor is, therefore, a percentage of 8 000 lux. To get daylight factors from lux values of illumination levels for various industrial tasks and locations given in Table 1, divide these values by 80. As an example, if an illumination level required at a point inside a building is, say, 300 Iux, the daylight factor 300 required would be= = 3.75, that is, 3.75 per cent of the illumination obtained outdoor from unobstructed direct sunlight being sky, excluded. 5.2.1 Daylight reaching an indoor reference point comprises the light from the following Sources: a) The direct ( excluding sky visible from direct sun ), the point the sky component ( SC ), the external reflected component ( ERC ) and the internal reflected component ( IRC ) of the daylight factor. total daylight factor ( DF ) is Therefore, the sum of the sky component ( SC ), the external reflected component ( ERG ) and the internal reflected component ( IRC), or DF = SC + ERC + IRC As a conservative estimate, only the sky component is taken into consideration for the purpose of designing fenestrations of the factory buildings. However, other components are also important from the point of view of reducing glare and ensuring brightness contrasts between the objects and the surroundings, and these should be taken into consideration for the quality of the lighting required in the interiors. 5.2.2 No standard of daylighting for factories in terms of daylight factors is laid down in the Factories Act ( 1948 ). In Model Rule 29 framed by the Central Government under the Act, a minimum standard of 30 lux is laid down as a general level of illumination for the working areas of a factory. This standard is without prejudice to the provision of any additional illumination required for the work itself. Cleariy this value refers only to illumination from artificial sources and is not really applicable to daylighting. The standard may be taken to correspond to a daylight factor of a little over 0.5 percent for overcast sky during the monsoon months when the outside intensities fall to about 5 000 lux. This can be obtained in practice by an area of roof glazing as small as 2.5 percent of the floor area. In existing factories, glass areas are seldom less than 10 percent, and the daylight factors of 2.5 percent and more are common. In normal circumstances factories should be designed to give at least 1.25 percent daylight factor, which may exceed current requirements over part or whole of the building. The lesser value would certainly be considered inadequate. 5.2.3 The openings, glazings and such similar sources of daylighting should be so positioned as to give levels of illumination given in Table 1 expressed as daylight factors. The area of glazing or opening required for any particular level of illumination will depend primarily upon the position of fenestration adopted. The relative efficiency of different methods may be compared by calculating the ratio of the glazed area to floor area in each case. For analysis of daylight in factories, Central Building Research Institute has developed daylight protractors for estimation of direct component of daylight factor. These are for determination of sky ( direct ) component for clear design sky at any point on a horizontal plane, a vertical plane normal to window glazing and a vertical plane parallel to window glazing. The protractors have the particular

In the Handbook on Functional Requirements in Buildings other than Industrial Buildings,* some examples have been given to determine the sky components ( from clear design sky ) inside the building by the use of protractors. The same method of design will apply in case of factory buildings which are multistoreyed and have provision for daylighting through windows and louvers in the side walls. 5.2.4 A careful interpretation of daylight factors should be made before designing the fenestration. The possibility that the required level of illumination may change due to change in the layout caused by modification in production methods should be kept in view. Obstructions like structural members, overhead installations, vertical and horizontal machines and the like should be considered in relation to the glazing. It is essential to foresee the proposed layout of the machines, as ignorance of this aspect is likely to cut down the light reaching the workplace. There should be good distribution of light over the whole interior. Unilateral systems should, therefore, be avoided when possible. Light colours should predominate on the surface of the interior, wherever practicable. 5.3 Daylight Fenestration - For the purpose of daylight fenestration, the factory buildings may be grouped into three types; buildings with skylight, buildings with closed ceilings ( as in multistoreyed buildings ), and high-bay large span structures. 5.3.1 Buildings with Skylight

North ) may be ascertained from the table. Indiscriminate use of north lights in places. located south of 23" latitude should be avoided. In South India the use of northlighting is highly questionable unless some special forms of diffusing glasses are also used to cut off direct entry of sunlight. The second method of fenestration by skylight is when double-pitched ( gabled roof ) trusses are used so that glazing may be distributed on one or both pitches. One more method which is not so common in India is where the roof glazing is arranged in opposite vertical strips in a system known as. `Monitor' roofing. 5.3.1.2 Before further discussing the methods. of fenestration as given in 5.3.1.1 for the purpose of providing daylight in factory buildings, it must be remembered that the area of the glazing required for any particular level of illumination will depend primarily upon the position of the fenestration adopted. The relative efficiency of different methods for a particular type of building may be compared by calculating the ratio of the glazed area to floor area in each case. Methods using horizontal or low-pitched glazing will generally be more efficient than those using vertical or steeply sloping glass. Allowance should be made in designing area of glazing for anything that may obstruct the light, such as tall buildings, overhead equipment and large machines. Allowance should also be made for dust or dirt accumulated on glazing, which should of course be regularly cleaned and means of safe and easy access provided for the purpose. In the distribution curves for different types of roof fenestrations discussed in 5.3.1.3 to 5.3.1.5, the value of O-85 has been assumed for glass transmission and values of daylight factors include sky and reflected components for the clear design sky. 5.3.1.3 Saw-tooth ( north-light ) fenestrution

5.3.1.1 Where skylight is utilised, it is, as already mentioned, done in a way to avoid the effect of direct sunlight. Direct sunlight should be screened as far as possible. The alternative is to make use of diffusing materials of low transmittance for glazing those areas where the possibility of direct sunlight is high. The glazed areas are generally oriented away from the sunny side; thus in the northern hemisphere they face north. In this way a natural lighting is obtained of a diffused quality and with less variation of colour than is inherent in direct sunlight. Most factories employ north light as the principle source of daylighting. This is achieved by roofs of single-pitched truss of the saw-tooth type, where the glazing is oriented in north only. These keep off direct mid-day sun in latitudes north of 23". It is useful to know the period of the day over which direct sunlight enters such fenestration; this is shown in Table 3. types of north-light roofs include cylinderical shell or the Z-folded plate The structural requirement type. of the Z-folded plate limits the horizontal parts to 60-100 cm and slants of the the window and roof to about 80" and 40" to the horizontal respectively. The former usually takes the north-light openings. Studies at Central Building Research Institute, Roorkee, show that while these types of roofs are similar in their behaviour in relation to their sky components at any given point for the same vertical glazed areas, there are variations of the reflected components giving rise to differences in the ultimate performance of each one of the roofs. The Z-folded plate is almost similar to the saw-tooth when the glazed areas are similar but the cylindrical shell is inferior in that the level of illumination inside is less. For this type of roof the internal reflected component ( IRC ) is progressively less with increase in bay width beyond 5 m and the decrease is proportional to bay width thereafter so that when bay width is 13 m, it is nearly onehalf.

Example 1 - Determine the fenestration percent for obtaining 500 lux on the floor for (a) poor (b) good maintenance conditions in a 8-bay north-light factory building of 7 m bay width and 5 m sill height.

a) To account for the poor maintenance the workplane illuminance should be 500/0*7 = 715 lux.

In America the monitor roofs seem to have largely taken the place of northlight or saw-tooth roofs. The use of monitor roof is not very common in this country since the monitor openings also let in considerable quantities of direct sunlight which may be objectionable. However, the system has certain commendable features. For example, glass cleaning is straight forward, not involving special gantry equipment, and if opening lights can be suitably arranged, the inside face of the glass may also be cleaned from the outside. Because the glass is vertical, the periods between cleaning can probably be longer.

17

SP : 32 - 1986 b) General
level of illumination of monitor roof is low compared with other systems considered. This may be seen by the illumination distribution curve in Fig. 7 where a vertical glazing of 30 per cent of the floor area hardly gives between 7 and 6 percent daylight factor, compared with 9 and 6 percent for north-light roof with 20 percent glazing. Figure 8, however, shows that when the monitor roof glazing is sloping at 60' to the horizontal, the level of illumination goes up and, even with only 16 percent area of glazing, is between 7 and 5 percent daylight factor, though with this type of sloping monitor, the distribution is not so even. The monitor roof will give satisfactory results only if a succession of vertical glazings is used and then, over a large area, a very uniform distribution of light will result. Using of miniature louvers in conjunction with th.e glazing apertures with the louvers tilted by 45" to the horizontal may tend to send the light flux from the openings towards the ceiling of the monitor which in turn will diffusely illuminate the working plane. The ultimate working plane illumination will depend on the louver dimensions, spacing, reflectances, the interior surface finishes as well as the availability of daylight outdoors. The width of the monitor has also critical effect upon the influx distribution and, within limits, the monitor should in most cases be quite narrow. The glazed areas are then brought nearer to the areas between the monitors, SO increasing the illumination in the region. Care should also be taken to avoid- obstructing; the daylight by roof overhangs or projecting gutters. These the light may seriously diminish immediately beneath the monitor. If it is desired to reduce the more marked effects of sunshine penetration, monitor lighting should be laid out on a north-south axis. A good proportion of high angle hot noon sun will then be excluded, and further, early morning, late afternoon and winter sunshine coming at a flat angle will mostly be prevented from hitting the working plane. 5.3.1.5 Double-pitch inclined roof or horkontal rooffenestration

a) In either of these types of openings direct sun-light will be incident on the fenestrations for part or most of the daytime. This type of construction is employed when some direct incursion of daylight is permissible or uniformity of lighting is not critical as in the case of large warehouses. The design will have to be for the design time suggested in IS : 2440-1975*. The value of the total illumination to sun and skylight may be taken as 10 000 lux. To etfectively diffuse this illumination in the interior the use of diffusing glass or transluscent materials of known transmission factors is recommended. 5.3.2 Buildings with Closed Ceilings 5.3.2.1 For factory buildings with closed ceilings as in multi-storeyed buildings side glazing is the only answer for daylighting. This is similar to vertical windows and hence the methods given in IS : 2440- 1975% are directly applicable. The daylighting at any point inside the building is treated in the same manner as in a roof. In working areas with closed ceiling, the width is apt to be so large that the windows in the walls are proportionately too sufficient natural lighting low to provide At a depth of in the centre of the room. twice the window height, the horizontal illumination amounts to no more than 10 percent of that near the window and beyond a depth of about 8 m only reflected component of daylight can reach, and therefore, in many situations artificial lighting has to be empioyed during day time as well to suppleqtnt daylighting. 5.3.2.2 Unilateral lighting from side openings will in general be unsatisfactory if the effective width of the room is more than twice Openings on two the height of the opening. opposite sides will give greater uniformity of internal daylight illumination specially when the room is 8 m or more across. Crosslighting with openings on adjacent walls will tend to increase the diffused lighting within the factory shed. Openings should be provided with louvers, baffles or other shading devices to exclude, as far as possible, direct sunlight into the building. *Guide for daylighting of buildings ( second revision ).

FIG. 13 SIDE GLAZING IN A MULTI-STOREY BUILDINGS( 50 PERCENTOF FLOOR AREA )

FIG. 14 SIDE GLAZING IN A MULTI-STOREY BUILDING ( GLASS AREA 74 PERCENTOF FLOOR AREA )

20

SP : 32 - 1986 5.3.2.4 Generally with side lighting, while taller openings give greater penetration, broader openings give better distribution. Broader openings may also be equally or more efficient provided their sills are raised by 30 to 60 cm above the working plane. However, it is to be noted that this raising of the sill level is likely to reduce ventilation at work level. Therefore, while designing side openings for ventilation also, a compromise may be made by providing the sill height about 15 cm below the average head level of workers, so that the incoming air stream is passed over the workers. 5.3.2.5 In this type of construction it is less the daylighting than the tasks that are the determining factors. Situations may also arise where total exclusion of daylight may offer the only optimal solution to lighting design of industrial areas. Considerations such as heat loads due to sunlight, and of the areas or special requirements of production processes and the cost of air-conditioning the area may be the deciding factors, and the solution may lie in providing artificial illumination from the ceiling ,designed purely on the needs of the nature of work and layout. 5.3.3 High-bay Large S'an Structures of fenestrating. In the case of shell concrete construction, which is eminently suitable for covering extensive areas, the thin skin of reinforced concrete is structural and may not be pierced with impunity. In cases of dome-like structures with single large spans, the tendency should be to distribute the glazing in comparatively small individual areas rather than in large single panels which would break the structural continuity of the system. Alternati. vely, if the shell is formed in the vault, the glass may be arranged in more or less continuous narrow strips which follow the roof curve. In both cases the daylight distribution can be very even and intensities as high as 10 percent daylight factor. In case of structures with more than one span, the shell may be designed as a series ofbalanced cantilevers in either direction of each span, in which case a wide strip of glass running continuously down the crown of the vault is provided. In this type of structure also, with series of such roofs the daylight distribution of the order of 15 percent daylight factor in the middle of each bay with sloping of the curve to a value around 10 percent between the bays can be expected at the working plane. 5.4 Quality of Daylighting - Apart from provision of sufficient light which is uniformly distributed over the whole working area, an important aspect of daylighting of factory buildings is whether eyes of the workers can take good advantage of the light which is available in the building. In particular, as pointed out earlier, if the brightness ratios or contrast in the visual field are unsatisfactory, the retina of the eye will lose sensitivity, and vision will be both less satisfactory and less comfortable. The chief factor to be reckoned with, particularly when considering the design of the environment as a whole, is that the eye cannot comfortably adapt itself to strong contrast of brightness and glare. As has already been mentioned, glare is caused when sky is viewed through some glazed opening when the area of wall or roof around the opening is dark. The cure for this trouble is to surround the openings with surfaces which are light-coloured and wellilluminated. Certain forms of fenestration of factory buildings are much easier to treat this way than others. Both the north-light and the monitor roofs are, by the arrangement of their roof planes, less glaring than any of the orher types because the undersides of the roofs surrounding the glass can either be illuminated directly from the sky or can receive light by reflection from adjacent external roofs if these It is a common observation are light-coloured. that in a north-light factory the view facing the glazing is usually very uncomfortable compared with a view in the opposite direction when it is the underside of the roofs which are risible and not the sky. This is what would be expected, for where the bright sky is replaced by a

5.3.3.1 So far, the fenestrating of only the more common forms of factory buildings has been considered. Some attention should be directed to the daylighting of the kind of factories where provision of a large and unobstructed floor space is essential and smoother production flow and greater flexibility, in which the process is likely to be changed at some future date, is needed. The floor-to-roof height of such structures is high enough to provide clearance for the big jobs like assembly of aircraft, or accommodate overhead cranes, or to allow the fumes and steam from the processes to be carried off. In such factories it is usually possible to provide sufficient daylighting which would enter through the windows in the relatively high walls. Glass strips in the roof, when artificial lighting is required, would usually be installed as high as possible in the roof structure so as to allow unobstructed manipulation with cranes and assembly jobs. Due to high mounting of light sources the horizontal illumination is much more than the vertical illumination. When in particular cases, a high level of illumination in the vertical plane is required, a portion of the light sources are also mounted half-way between floor and roof against the walls or the wall columns. These are to be ,carefully screened to secure unobstructed view of the working space. 5.3.3.2 Where the spans are very large, the requirements of daylighting may impose limitations of a free choice of possible structures, or, conversely, the structural arrangement which is to be used may limit the method

21

SP : 32 - 1986 less bright ceiling the condition is bound to present less contrast than the other with just as much light on the work. In certain factories the risk of glare to workers operating machines or on the work benches may thus be reduced by different arrangement of the work benches and machines. The other method of reducing contrast will be to allow the roof glazing to run to the end walls; thereby surfaces around the glazing which might otherwise be in shadow are avoided. It should also be noted that merely by increasing the amount of light entering a room the general contrast between indoor and outdoor illumination may be reduced and the risk of window glare may thereby be lessened. In many cases this means that if an adequate quantity of light is reached the worst conditions of contrast will be automatically avoided. 6. ARTIFICIAL LIGHTING 6.1.2 Quality Artificial lighting may. to be provided as local also be required lighting when visual task may demand higher levels of illumination than are possible by general lighting. It must be designed to satisfy both quantity and quality for the industrial tasks in view. As already pointed out, quality relates to colour diffusion, direction ( where important ), direct and reflected glare and other factors that affect the degree of comfort for the worker. Quality is also influencenvironment or ed considerably by visual surrounding area within the field of view. 6.1.3 Layout While planning artificial lighting, the layout of the light fittings has to be related to the layout of the working area so as to obtain the most favourable lighting effect. for comfortable working. 6.2 Other Requirements Although colour of light emitted by a light source of an ob.ject does not affect the performance of a visual task, from psychological point of view, for tropical country like in India, cool colours such as green and buff are desirable for walls and machines with cool white light ( fluorescent, mercury vapour, etc ) from the light sources. Diffusion is important for general lighting except for certain specific applications, such as inspection work where directional control aids in seeing flaws quickly and easily. Large-area light sources and an upward component of light directed towards the ceiling aids diffusion, Direct glare is controlled by shielding with louvers, shields or other means. Reflected glare is diminished by large-area light sources of low brightness or by diffusing media, such as glass or plastics. 6.3 Types of Light Sources There are mainly three types of light sources for industry: Incandescent a> lamps; ( tungsten filament

6.1 While discussing task illumination levels, it was pointed out that artificial lighting may be provided to obtain the recommended illumination levels or general levels of lighting at the working plane when daylighting is not available or is inadequate, in the latter case to supplement daylighting. 6.1.1 Permanent Supplementary Lighting In work areas in which daylighting alone will not be adequate as, for instance, in deep multi-storeyed buildings, a permanent supartificial lighting installation plementary ( PSALI ) is provided. This system used in conjuncticn with daylighting ensures lighting which is more or less uniform throughout the day and is conducive to better efficiency and output. Specially where depths greater than say 12 m in buildings with ceiling heights of 3 m are encountered, such a system of artificial lighting becomes a necessity. The requirement of supplementary artificial lighting increases with the increase in availability of daylight. The design requires a careful analysis of the spacing of artificial light sources and no general solutions are, therefore, available. This system can also be integrated with artificial lighting for the night only by suitable compromise in the illlumination levels desired.

6.3.2 By far the most suitable lamp for factory installations is the tubular fluorescent lamp because of its shape and many other .advantages, although its luminous efficiency is no higher than between 50 and 65 lm/w. But its highly-diffused radiation makes it economically unsuitable for high-bay factories. For factory building with large ceiling heights, such as foundries, steel mills, aircraft plants, where high lumen output is more important than colour, high pressure mercury vapour ( HPMV ) lamps are economically suitable. Sodium vapour lamps have limited applications for lighting of interiors due to their colour and are sometimes used for street lighting and yards in cold climates as they have an advant.age of penetration in foggy weather. Tungsten filament lamps have limited use in factory working areas because of their low efficiency, short life and eventual frequent replacement. These are mainly adopted for godowns because of their infrequent use and other places where the nature of work does not ,demand high illumination levels. Their application is also limited either to local lighting or where used in combination with fluorescent lamps for power factor improvement. 6.4 Types of Luminaires Filament, mercury or fluorescent lamps may have lumi.. naires of different types depending upon the industrial requirements. Luminaires may be enclosed, ventilated open or non-ventilated open type. In smoky and dusty areas such as steel mills, foundries, flour mills, and coal yards, enclosed luminaries are used. These are usually of heavy duty type with a gasketted glass cover .to protect the reflector and the light source from collection of dust and dirt. In humid atmospheres, such as steam processing, plating and washrooms also enclosed luminaries are used. Where heavy oils are used or processed and oil mists are generated, vapour-tight fix23

tures should be used. Flame-proof fittings are required for explosive atmospheres. In highbay areas, ventilated type luminaries are generally preferred rather than non-ventilated type, because the dust collected on luminaires is cleaned automatically by fast rising air currents. In high narrow areas, luminaires having a concentrating or medium-spread distribution produce illumination on the horizontal plane most economically. In high wide areas, widespread distribution provides good illumination. Luminaires near the walls may have narrower distribution to minimise light losses through windows and walls. In low-bay areas either a grid arrangement ( continuous rows at right angles ) or continuous rows of fluorescent luminaires are installed. These may be of the direct or semi-indirect type shielded by louvers, baffles or other devices. 6.5 Interior Lighting Design - For general lighting purposes in industrial areas, the recommended practice is to design for a level of illumination on the working plane on the basis of the recommended levels for different visual tasks given in Table 1. A method called luminous flux method or simply, lumen method, is emplyed to provide for a uniform distribution of light over the entire work area. This method of designing the interior lighting systems for various types of luminaires and conditions of the rooms and their surroundings is described in 6.5.1 to 6.5.6. 6.5.1 The initial luminous flux output of a few common incandescent and fluorescent lamps is known and is given in Table 7. Luminaires are classified into five categories as given in Table 8 in accordance with the flux output above and below the horizontal. The luminous flux reaching the workplace both directly from the luminaire and by reflection and inter-refiection from walls and ceilings is determined by

SP:32 -1986
the type of luminaire, room index and the reflectances of room surfaces. The ratio of this flux reaching the working plane and the flux generated by the lamps is known as coefficient of utilization. Room index classifications are based on room ratios which are calculated in terms of room dimensions and mounting height. For direct, semi-direct and diffuse luminaires, Room index = Width x length Mounting height above working plane x ( Width + length ) 6.5.3 Lumens reaching the working plane due to a number of lamps or luminaires, say .N, each having luminous flux output, say F, will be N x F x C x M, where C is the coeffici-, ent of utilization and 1V.fthe maintenance factor for the luminaire in given room surroundings.. This must be equal to total luminous flux required for a given ( average ) illumination intensity level EAV for a room of area A, that is, EAv x A. If illumination of required level is required at specific points, calculations are made by the point-by-point method. It requires the computation of direct illumination due to given light sources at specific points and adding to it the indirect illumination due to inter-reflection at that point. For the computation of direct illumination, a source is treated as a surface source or a point source depending upon whether or not the inverse square law ( for point source ) is obeyed. 6.5.7 Inverse square law holds good for most sources at a distance greater than five times the largest dimension of the source. Sky factors can be used for determining illuminance at any point due to uniformly diffusing plane surface sources. Most of the large surface sources may be approximated as plane surface and may be assumed to be uniformly diffusing. 6.6

6.6.1 In some industrial operations, like pouring of molten metal and moulding in steel mills, sand blasting in foundries, drawing-in process in textile mills, lighting is provided by means of fixed or adjustable reflectors designed to focus a high intensity over a small work area and to supplement general lighting. Sometimes this type of lighting is provided locally for viewing difficult industrial tasks or inspection processes in metal shops or machine shops that cannot be illuminated satisfactorily or practically by the general lighting system. 7. MAINTENANCE 7.1 Regular
maintenance of lighting installations including all windows and skylights glazings cannot be neglected without prejudicing the level of illumination and hence the benefits that accrue from good lighting. Table 10 shows that the maintenance problem in factories is an extremely important one. It will be seen that in certain cases, half the light emitted is absorbed by dust accumulated on the light sources over a period of three months. It is important to maintain the colour of the walls and other reflecting surfaces when colour rendering has been a design consideration.

. cl) Low brightness
equipment usually in the form of uniform luminous panel.

6.6.2 These luminaires are preferably mounted on the machine or at the location where they are used. They are sometimes provided with movable arms or swivel arrangements for individual adjustment. Under some circumstances, for example where repair work is being done on automobiles, heavy machines or aeroplanes or work is being done in confined spaces, portable lighting equipment which can be moved in any direction, is to be used. Portable lamps should be properly earthed, insulated or double-insulated and preferably be of low voltage ( 25 volts ). 6.6.3 Some special industrial require use of special colour lamps, or nal lighting for detection of flaws texture, or ultra-voilet lighting for chemicals or for detection. processes directioin cloth analysing

8. CONCLUSION

8.1 The

6.7 Emergency Lighting - Failure at night of the main lighting supply in and around factory premises where work is in progress can result in serious danger. The risk is greater where there are moving machinery, open tanks or vats. Emergency lighting installations become necessary for such situation. Emergency lighting is also important in power stations to allow safe access to the plant for the purpose of restoring the supply following a breakdown.

lighting of factory buildings is often considered to be of less importance than that of office and residential buildings. However, if the requirements imposed by the work which is to be carried on for 8 hours in a day or shift are taken into consideration, it will be realised that for many industrial locations and processes, vrsual acquity of high order is required so as to make the work more efficient and productive. The improvement in methods of factory lighting which has been possible over recent years clearly shows that the critical lighting requirements are appreciated and accepted by factory managements.

8.2 The uti!ization of daylight is recommended as a first step for the sake of economy and availability. Design of fenestrations is important. Other lighting systems, either supplementary to daylighting or otherwise have to be designed to go along well with the visual tasks required to be performed in the factory.

SP I 32 - 1986 SECTION 9. INTRODUCTION 2 VENTILATION
The amount of air required depends on the air space available per person and the degree of physical activity, and, when there are no contaminants to be removed from the air of a workplace, it may vary from 20 ms to 30 ms per person per hour, the amount increasing as the air space per person decreasing. Under the Facto&s Act, I984 no standard has been laid down as regards fresh air required per worker or amout of air change per hour. However, a standard for preventing overcrowding has been laid down under section 16, which requires that at least 14.16 ms of space shall be provided for every worker employed in a workplace, no account being taken of the space 4.25 m above the floor level. Considering this minimum requirement of air space per person, even a little over single air change per hour in a factory building is sufficient to take care of this provision. In actual practice, except for factories where a large number of sedentary workers work in crowded localities, such as Bidi factories, a much larger work space is provided in factories and this problem of vitiation of atmosphere by body odours does not arise. Air movement, however, is of importance to prevent stagnation and remove innocuous contaminants of no particular significance, and this can be achieved by mere air circulation by fans and air infiltration by natural means by keeping the windows and other openings open to the extent required depending on the season. X0.1.2.1 Vitiation of the atmosphere can also occur in a factory by odours given off due to contamination of the product itself, say for example, tobacco processing in a Bidi factory. Here the ventilation will have to be augmented or other methods employed to keep the odours to within unobjectionable levels. 10.1.3 Heat Balance of Body - A major consideration for providing ventilation is on based the process of heat regulation of human body and the role of air movement associated with it. As is well known, the human body tries to maintain a thermal equilibrium whereby a normal body temperature of 37�C is maintained. This is achieved by exchange of heat generated through metabolism with heat in the environment by the process of conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation. Conduction is not significant as this takes place only when the body is in physical contact with hot or cold bodies. The rest of the processes are expressed for the purpose of maintaining heat balance of the body, by the following equation: M-W=E&-R&C&S where M is the rate of metabolism, W is the units, 31 rate of work done in the heat

9.1 In a hot country like India,

special attention should be given to the requirements of ventilation in the design and layout of factory buildings so as to maintain such thermal environments as are conducive to the efficiency and Lye11 being of workers. This aspect is of particular importance in the case of factories, as in addition to the heat transmitted into the buildings from the sun, heat is added within the buildings as a result of manufacturing processes carried on in factories. When the temperatures inside the factory buildings are raised due to this excessive heat gain and the workers are required to perform heavy jobs manually, they not only suffer discomfort and heat stress, but their efficiency is also likely to be adversely affected. Observations in many industries have shown that workers' output undergoes a seasonal it is generally highest in winter, variation; lowest in summer and at an intermediate level betlveen the two in spring and autumn. In sumin factories mer, when thermal environments are worsened, an adequate supply of fresh air by ventilation from outdoors into the factory building: will help in relieving discomfort and distress. Ventilation is also required to remove dusts, gases, fumes and other contaminants from certain processes carried on in the factory buildings.

10;PHYSIOLOGICAL

CONSIDERATIONS

10.1Before we discuss the actual requirements and methods of ventilation in factory buildings, it is felt that a brief description of the physiological needs of workers from the point of view of ventilation and comfort would be useful. 10.1.1 Respiration - It used to be thought in earlier days that ventilation is necessary to supply fresh air for respiration to replenish oxygen required for life process and to maintain carbon dioxide concentration of the surrounding air within safe limits. It has been found, however, that from purely physiological consideration, the concentration of carbon dioxide in ambient air, until it reaches the level of 3 percent, is incapable of producing any harmful effect, whereas in closed rooms, it seldom exceeds 0.04 percent due to existence of air leaks through crevices and other openings in buildings. Similarly as regards oxygen, until its concentration goes below I4 percent in air, no untowardsymptoms are likely to be felt whereas existence of air leaks in buildings seldom allows it to drop below 19 percent which is well above the margin of oxygen deficiency.
10.1.2 Vitiation by Body Odours - Another consideration for providing ventilation in a building is. the dilution of inside air to prevent vitiation of the atmosphere by body odours.

SP : 32 -

1986
11. STANDARDS OF TEMPERATURE

E is the rate of evaporative heat loss, R is the rate of radiation heat loss or
gain, C is the rate gain, and of convective storage heat loss or

S is the rate of heat

in the body.

There are formulae to work out the actual rate of heat gain or loss by the various processes, but this is beyond the scope of discussion here. However, it is sufficient 10 mention that body heat metabolism increases with the environmental temperature and the degree of phys ical activity and this must be balanced by body heat gain or loss by other means as given in the equation. In hot environments in factories when air temperatures are much above the body temperature ( skin temperature j the body begins to gain heat also through process of radiation and convection, and this also requires to be offset, and the only way is by the process of evaporation of sweat from the body. In humid environments, there is reduction in the loss of heat by evaporation. The body will attempt to balance the heat gain by perspiring to increase evaporation. When the heat is not dissipated to balance the heat gain of the body, heat may get stored in the body and manifest itself by rise in body temperature above the normal, 35�C. This imbalance may cause discomfort and injury to health such as by heat stroke and heat collapse. Here one can see the influence of providing air movement and of ventilation in air temperature by means relieving heat stress. Ventilation will help in taking away heat load in factory buildings and thus bring down the temperature to near the temperature of the outside air. In hot workplaces, air movement over the body will facilitate evaporation of sweat and help in maintaining heat balance. However, care must be exercised in using very high velocities when the temperature of the air exceeds skin temperature, 35"c, because convective heat is then added to any existing radiative heat, at these, together with metabolic heat, must be removed by evaporation of sweat to maintain body heat balance. While increased velocity will.also increase evaporation Of sweat, a critical point is reached when addition of convective heat will exceed the removal of heat by tvaporation. There is experimental evidence to show that increase in the air velocity up to about 150 metres per minute will only enhance sweating but will not cause rise in body temperature or pulse rate of the workers irrespective of high temperatures prevailing in many workplaces. When air velocities higher than these are used, it should be ensured that the actual rise in body temperature or pulse rate of workers does not exceed the normal to an alarming degree. Only of extreme dry heat, there in environments might be need for cooling the air ( see 16 and 17 ) before it is let into the workplace.

11.1 From the foregoing discussion, it is clear that for a proper exchange of heat from or to the surroundings to take place, the temperature and humidity of the ambient air with respect to that of the body ( or skin ) are important. The thermal environmental factors affecting this heat exchange are temperature of the ambient air ( as measured by ordinary dry-bulb thermometer ), relative humidity of air or wet-bulb temperature (as measured by wet-bulb thermometer ), rate of air movement near the body and the amount of heat radiation from the surroundings [ as measured indirectly by black globe thermometer ). A number of indices of thermal comfort or of heat tolerance in terms of these environmental factors or in terms of sweat rate and other factors have been suggested by the researchers. 11.2 A more commonly used index called effective temperature, combining air temperature, relative humidity and air movement gives sensory scale of warmth of air felt by the human body and denotes the temperature of saturated air under still-air conditions in which an equivalent sensation of warmth is experienced by majority of persons. As clothing will influence the thermal feeling, two scales, one for subjects dressed in customary indoor winter clothing performing light work ( see Fig. 15 for normal scale ) and the other for subjects stripped to waist and at rest ( see Fig. 16 for basic scale ) have been developed. The scales are corrected for radiation by making use of globe thermometer temperature instead of dry-bulb temperature when radiation from solid surroundings is present. 11.3 Considering only the thermal factors, comfort conditions are those under which a person can maintain normal balance between production and loss of heat at normal body temperature and without perceptable sweating. Limits of comfort vary considerably according to the studies carlied out in this country and abroad. A detailed discussion of these and comfort zones for various parts of the world is beyond the scope of this handbook. In this country it has been found that for affording reasonable comfort to workers for everyday work of moderate intensity and for efficient production in factories, an effective temperature of the ambient air in summer should not exceed 27�C. 11.4 When in certain industrial processes excessive temperatures prevail and the degree of physical activity is high, conditions are beyond comfort limits and physiological limit of heat tolerance by workers may be reached. This limit is determined when the bodily heat balance is upset, that is, beyond this limit the bodily heat gain exceeds bodily heat loss and profuse sweating occurs.

FIG. 15 CHART SHOWING NORMAL SCALE OF CORRECTED EFFECTIVE ( OR EFFECTIVE ) TEMPERATURE 11.5 An index which is applicable to worksituations in factories where sweating occurs and temperatures are fairly high is the predetermined four-hour sweat rate ( P4SR ) which is found empirically from a nomogram based on thermal environmental factors, amount of physical activity and clothing worn by workers. A sweat rate of 4.5 litres in four hours is the upper limit of tolerence for work in hot environment. On grounds of efficiency and health, a sweat rate of 2.5 litres in four hours is considered optimal for workers of European stock. For metal workers doing light work ( about 230 watts work rate), this sweat rate corresponds to a limiting effective temperature of about 30�C. For sedentary work ( about 115 watts work rate ), the limit may be exceeded to about 33.5%. 33 11.6 Studies on Indian workers well acclimatized, wearing light clothing and doing work of moderate severity ( about 350 watts work rate ) have shown that the limits of heat tolerance for dry heat are 46�C dry-bulb and 32% wet-bulb and for wet heat, 35.6% dry-bulb and 33.3% wet-bulb, but since the studies were conducted on workers of good physique, these limits have been lowered, somewhat arbitrarily, and `upper safe limits' in terms of maximum permissible wet-bulb temperature corresponding to a given dry-bulb temperature have been suggested, as in Table I 1. 12. CONTROL OF HEAT

12.1 Application of ventilation in factory buildings should be preceded by and considered alongwith the measures to control heat which

SP:32-1988
may otherwise give rise to excessively high temperatures. Besides the solar heat, the main sources of heat in factories are the hot processes, such as work near furnaces, kilns, molten metal, forgings, etc, and the processes which are both hot and humid, such as calendering work in textile mills, vats, etc. It is neither economical nor feasible to stop escape of all the process heat or to offset it completely by the usual methods of ventilation. The measures to control such heat will not only facilitate better design of ventilation but also reduce their cost. The various methods of control of and protection against heat exposures are discussed in 12.1.1 to 12.1.7. 12.1.1 Solar I-hat-In tropics, new buildings should be oriented for minimum solar load during summer, so that less heat is transmitted through walls and ceiling. Consistant with .the requirements of ventilation there should be minimum number of windows on the south and west walls, and the roofs should be inclined away from the sun rays. For this reason, the factory buildings in northern parts of India are mostly north-light roofed buildings. To avoid heat due to solar radiation on roofs from being reradiated and transmitted into the factory buildings, roof should either be made of insulating materials or a false ceiling or double roof with a well-ventilated air

It is recommended that an insulation lining of 2.5 to 5 cm thickness ofsuitable material equvalent to not more than 2.30 W/( ma "C ) heat transmission coefficient for the composite roof be provided on the roof of corrugated iron or corrugated asbestos or other thin sheets. Some reduction can also be achieved by painting the roof with white paint or white wash or with other heat Roof could also be of alumireflecting paints. nium sheets which have high reflectivity to solar radiation even after they get old. 1261.3 Insulation - The insulation of furnaces and other heat-producing equipment including pipes, vessels and vats will not only reduce the amount of heat exposure but also result in the consequent saving in fuel consumption of the equipment. But the mere insulation will be of no value unless the heat produce and dissipated into the building escapes through ventilation. This may be by gravity through roof or by exhaust ventilation over the hot processes. 12.1.4 Substitution - Sometimes, it is possible to substitute a hot process by a method that involves application of localised or more efficiently controlled method of heating. Examples include induction furnaces instead of conventional heating furnaces, cold-rivetting or spot welding instead of hot-rivetting, etc. 12.1.5 Radiation Shielding - Hot processes like furnaces and hot surfaces such as layers of molten metal ( emanating radiant heat ) can best be controlled by placing a shield having a highly reflecting surface between the source of heat and the workers so that a major portion of the heat falling on the shield is reflected back to the surface and only a small percentage reradiated and transmitted ( emitted ) into the working atmosphere. Since the heat emitted by the shielding material depends on its temperature ( absolute ), it should not be in direct contact with the hot surface SO that it becomes a secondary sources of radiant heat. An intervening space should be provided and

12.1.2 Isolation - As regards the heat generated by hot processes within the factory building, the first obvious step is to eliminate the heat sources wherever possible or to isolate or segregate them. Thus, some of the hot equipment could be placed out of doors with only a protective roof. The location of furnaces in separate wings of the factory rather than in a large single building will simplify the problem of ventilation of the rest of the building. Some such equipment may be located in

35

SP : 32 - 1966
provision made for free flow upwards of the air heated in the space between the hot surface and the shield ( see Fig. 17 ). Sheets of tin and aluminium are employed as shield which are either placed permanently in closed proximity with the hot surface or moved from place to place to intervene the hot processes from the workers. 12.1.6 Local Relief - In certain situations when a general reduction of heat exposures throughout the building interior is not feasible and all the above methods of control may not help in bringing down the thermal environments to a tolerable degree, relief may be provided locally, that is, at the workplaces by surrounding the exposed workers with an acceptable environment either by providing a complete enclosure fully air conditioned or separately ventilated, or by surrounding the workers with a relatively cool atmosphere through a direct supply of cool air at the working level or by directing high velocity The Iast method is used to proman-coolers. vide `spot cooling' in large space where scattered work spots and localised sources of heat make it highly impracticable to maintain a tolerable environment throughout the space. 12.1.7 Personal Protection - Where operations do not permit high velocity air stream or (spot cooling' and where hot work is carried on in confined spaces, protective clothing or shielding of heat reflecting type or air-cooled suits are the only effective means found for protecting the workers from highly abnormal heat exposures. 13. OF VENTILATION

13.1 Meteorological data show that both in hot arid regions and in coastal areas in summer, the air temperatures are generally lower than the safe upper limits, and therefore, an adequate supply of outside air by ventilation will help in relieving the thermal stress caused from indoor conditions which are worsened by heat generated from machinery and hot processes. Ventilation has, therefore, three main functions to performbringing down the temperature inside the building closer to that outside, distributing the air satisfactorily throughout the building interiors and maintaining an adequate air movement at places of work. Although every case has to be studied according to the conditions prevailing, the amount of ventilation ( the quantity of air in cubic metres per minute ) is governed chiefly by the size of the building space and itsiusage, duration and type of occupancy and the nature of the activities, total amount of sensible heat gained from sun through walls, roof, windows, and other openings, and that generated from equipment, processes, lights and occupants, and temperature conditions desired to be maintained inside the building space at the working level in relation to those of outside air, and is given by the formula:

Only when natural ventilation fails to provide adequate thermal and environments that mechanical means of ventilation may be employed.
