14.1 Forces which operate to induce ventilation in a building are due to:

13.3 The larger of the two values worked out on the basis of both sensible heat and latent heat load should be used in actual practice. However, in majority of the cases, the sensible heat gain will far exceed the latent heat gain so that the amount of air required can be calculated in most cases on the basis of the first equation. These formulas are applicable for working out ventilation rates either by natural ventilation or mechanical ventilation. 13.4 Ventilation is also expressed in terms of cubic metreslhour per square metre of the floor area. This relationship fails to evaluate the actual heat relief provided by a ventilation system, but it does give a relationship which is independent of building height. This is a more rational approach because; with the same internal load, the same amount of ventilation air, properly applied to the work zone with adequate velocity, will provide the desired heat relief quite independently of the ceiling height. Ventilation rates of 30 to 60 ms/h per ms of work area have been found to give good results in many plants. 13.5 Many text books give values of heat gain by solar radiation through walls, roofs windows

pressure exerted by the wind outside, that is, wind action. This causes the outside air to enter the building, pass over the working area and then leave on other side of the building.

b) temperature

difference of the air within and without the building, that is, thermal head. This causes warm air to move upwards by convection ( stack action or chimney effect ) wherefrom it leaves the building through the openings in or near the roof and is replaced by comparatively cool air entering the building at lower levels through windows or louvers.

14.1.1 In many parts of this country, in winter, thts difference in temperature inside and outside a factory building is usually adequate to induce a sufficient rate of ventilation and air movement for winter comfort. In fact, it may even lead to draughts which may be minimised by keeping the inlet openings partially closed. In summer, however, the temperature within a factory building at the working level is not usually higher than 3�C in excess of that in a shade outside except near hot objects and equipment generating or radiating heat. Therefore, unless the building has sufficient thermal head due to such `hot' processes being carried on therein, the ventilation due to stack action or chimney effect generally will be less and

37.

SP : 32 - 1986 may not be sufficient for providing comfort to the occupants. reasonable to conjecture that it is in the region of 30 m beyond which sufficient reliance can not be placed on prevailing winds. Approximately half the ventilating area of openings should be between floor level and a height of 2.25 m from the floor, and so arranged that there will be passage of air across all parts of the building. The rest of the ventilating openings may be provided under the eaves to assist in windowto-ceiling cross ventilation. Direct short circuit between openings on two sides at high level may clear the air at the level without producing appreciable ventilation at the lower level of occupancy. A common mistake is to block the openings by placing a range of offices, latrine blocks or stairs along the greater part of the outside walls, thereby defeating the very purpose of the openings in the walls. When wind direction is not dependable the openings should be so arranged that as far as possible there is approximately an equal area on all sides of the building and all the openings are located at the same level near the occupants. Thus, no matter what the wind direction is, there are always some openings directly exposed to wind pressure and the others on leeward side to air suction and effective movement of air through the building is assured. 14.3 Roofed Ventilation - Cross ventilation by provision of windows and wall ventilators is suitable only for narraw factory buildings in which openings are provided at least on two opposite sides open to outside. When the buildings are wide as is the case in most of the singlestoryed factory buildings, good results can often be achieved by provision of roofed ventilation. Roofed ventilation can be designed either from the point of view of stack action for removal from floor level to roof, of smoke, fumes and other contaminants liberated during heat producing processes or for wind action to provide roof-to-floor ventilation when the manufacturing processes do not contribute appreciably to the heat of the environment. In the latter case, the principle involved is the same as in the case of cross ventilation, to make use of the high pressure on the windward side of the building and the reduced pressure on the leeward side to effect sufficient floor of air through the building. 14.3.1 Three types of buildings with roofs commonlv used in factories will be considered from the boint of view of natural ventilation: a) Double-pitched roofed building with a continuous ridge in the middle of each bay, Saw-tooth ing, and ( north-light ) roofed build-

14.1.2 Since thermal head caused by chimney effect can be set up only when heat producing equipment or processes are present inside a factory building, the factory buildings which do not have such `hot' processes, that is, buildings with assembly, fabrication or machinin.g jobs, special attention should be given to then design to provide wind action. Although the meteorological data for various cities and towns would show that wind forces are not consistent and vary both in intensity and direction, for design purposes, the wind may be assumed to come from one prominent direction either at right angle to one face of a building or obiiquely. The side from which the wind blows is called windward side, causing a positive pressure to be built up, and the opposite side from which wind leaves is called leeward side, building a negative pressure, and this difference in pressure creates the necessary draught of air through the building. If the wind is incident obliquely, say at an angie of 45" to one face of a building and therefore to the other adjoining face as well, the positive pressure will be built up on the two adjoining faces on the windward side and negative pressure on other leeward faces to cause necessary ventilation through the building. 14.2 Cross Ventilation Cross veutilation through one side of the building to the other can usually be obtained in narrow buildings of the width common in the multistoreyed type by the provision of large and suitably placed windows or combination of windows and wall ventilators for the inflow and outflow of air. Air movement will have to be sufficiently high during summer months to bring down the temperature of the inside air as nearly the same as that of the outside air. Although it is difficult to evolve a standard to determine the area of ventilating openings required for providing natural ventilation by cross ventilation through a building owing to large variation in climatic conditions, heat loads within a building and other physical factors, experience indicates that the size of the room may be taken as the basis. For narrow buildings having width not more than 25 m and where heat gain from manufacturing process or from radiating equipment is not much, the area of openings available for natural ( cross ) ventilation may, as a working rule, be 10 percent of the total floor area. For wider buildings, the area of openings will have to be increased so as to provide good amount of ventilation and air movement to reach the centre of the building. The data available do not permit precise determination of the maximum width up to which buildings of height usually found in factories may be extended while still being effectively ventilated by natural means by wind action, but it is reasonable

14.3.1 .l Double-pitched roofed building: a) No suction will be induced due to wind action in this type of building if the ridge has openings on both sides ( see Fig. 18 ) as the wind would pass through one side of the ridge to the other without any effect in the lower portion of the building. This type of roof is employed only if there is sufficient stack action inside the building and is effective for the removal of substantial and concentrated heat over open-hearth furnaces, soaking pits and glass furnances. However, when the ridge is provided with longitudinal baffles on both sides ( see Fig. 19 ), these baffles act as wind band which will cause the wind to jump over the ridge, and the attendant suction between the baffles will result in an upward movement of air from inside the building. Its capacity will increase with wind velocity. These types of stream lined ventilators are most suitable for highbay buildings and warehouses. On some of these buildings, instead of continuous ridge ventilators, cowl type ventilators or what is known as `Robertson' ventilators can be seen ( see Fig. 20 ). The circular wind band around each ventilator causes a wind jump resulting in an upward movement of air from within the building. The performance of roof-cowl ventilators depends on the difference between the temperature of the air inside and that outside, on the height of these ventilators above the air intake, on the velocity of the wind outside and on the crosssectional area of the ventilator, and is given by empirical equation: Q= where Qis rate of air flow in ms/min, A is cross sectional H is the height area in ms, inlets,in m, above A [ 8-O ,/ H (tl to) + 5-82 I'] ventilation than would otherwise be the possib!e with ventilator along ridge only. To ensure high level of performance it is essential that the height of the ventilators is sufficient say 10 m or more, above the low intakes, and the exit temperature is about 10�C above the prevailing outdoor temperature.

14.3.1.2 Saw-toothed ( north-light ) roofed building - The pattern of airflow produced in this type of building by wind forces is fairly complex, and varies with the proportions of the ridges, size and plan of the building itself and the direction of the wind, that is, whether it blows with, against or along the saw-teeth or obliquely. The inherent difficulty with this type of roof is that wind from north often creates down draughts into the building. To create upward clraughts for the removal of heat, smoke and fumes, a suitable modification in the shape of the saw-teeth ( see Fig. 21 ) is necessary so that wind blowing over the roof creates wind jump and causes an upward flow of air from the building and thus assists the flow due to thermal head of the building. In localities where southerly winds predominate in summer, the design of the north-light roofs

14.4 Amount of Air 14.4.1 By Wind Action - Rate of air flow by wind action when openings are provided both on the windward and leeward sides of the building is given by the expression: Q= 16.7 KAY where Q is the rate of air ilow, in ms/min, X is the coefficient of effectiveness, A is free area of inlet openings ( windward or leeward side ) in m*, and V is the wind velocity in km/h. The coefficient of effectiveness X depend upon the direction of wind relative to the openings. It varies from 0.5 to 0.6 for wind blowing perpendicular to the openings and from 0.25 to O-35 for wind blowing obliquely at 45' to the openings. 14.4.1.1 For wind data, local meterological office should be consulted. This equation is based on 65 percent effectiveness of openings. This percentage should be reduced to 50 percent if conditions are not favourable. .43

14.4.3 Combined Efect - When both the forces due to wind outside and temperature difference are acting together, the resulting airflow is not equal to the sum of the two quantities estimated from the above two equations. The flow through an opening is proportional to the square root of the sum of the two heads acting on that opening. When the air ilow due towind action and that due to temperature difference are equal and ventilating openings are operated so as to coordinate them, the total air-flow through the building is about 30 percent greater than that produced by either head acting independently under conditions ideal to it. This percentage decreases rapidly as one head increases over the other. The effect of the larger head will always predominate. The following simplified method is employed. Calculate the flow produced by each force seperately under conditions of openings best suited for coordination of forces. Determine the ratio of the flow produced by temperature difference to the sum of the two flows and find out the actual flow due to combined forces from the following table: Flow due to temperature difference ( convection effects ) as percentage of the total Actual flow as a multiple of the floor due to temperature difference 100 75 50 40 30 20

I n providmg mechanical ventilation, proper consideration should be given to the size and configuration of the building, the arrangement of inlet openings in relation to outlet openings, location and disposition of fans, air grilles and ductwork, if any, with due regard to manufacturing processes carried on. 15.2 Mechanical ventilation may be either (a) by exhaust whereby air is removed from a building by means of a fan while fresh air is introduced from windows and other openings, or (b) by positive ventilation whereby air is supplied by means of a fan or blower from outside, or (c) by combination of both exhaust and positive ventilaton. In case of positive ventilation, it is possible, where necessary, to cool the air before being brought into the building either by way of evaporative cooling or by airconditioning. 15.2.1

aggravated, and the existing system may often become ineffective. It has also been found that when the exhaust is insufficient, the workers complain of discomfort and open the windows on the side on which the fans are located. This causes what is known as `short-circuiting' of air as the air instead of being exhausted from the building is taken from the openings, thus defeating the very purpose for which exhaust fans are provided. This is a very common fault with this type of ventilation. The solution lies in keeping the openings on the side of the fans completely closed while the fans are working and augmenting the exhaust capacity so as to provide sufficient amount of air movement throughout the span of the building. 15.2.1.3 In a large building, exhaust ventilation can be provided by having a fan of adequate size connected to a ductwork alongside a wall with windows closed so that air is drawn across the building interior through the exhaust openings in the duct. The fan can be centrally located on an attic or other unused space and arranged to draw proportionately from several work areas of the building ( see Fig. 25 ). To overcome resistance of the ductwork, the fan may be of centrifugal type. Exhaust ventilation with ductwork may [also be applied to draw air from exhaust appliances to remove harmful dusts, fumes, etc, given off in manufacturing processes ( see 19.1 ). 15.2.2

Exhaust

Ventilation

15.2.1.1 Ventilation by this method can be efl'ected in the case of narrow buildings. Exhaust fans are provided in walls on one side of the building or in the attic and the roofs to draw large volumes of air through the building from the opposite side. These fans are usually of propeller type since they are required to operate against little or no resistance. Care should be taken to see that adequate inlet openings for air are provided so as to minimise draughts caused by high inlet velocities, and to avoid drop in the efficiency of the fans. The total inlet area should be at least three times the total disc area of the fans. 15.2.1.2 Location of the exhaust fans in relation to the inlet openings is important. If the building is later extended, the problem is

Positive Ventilation

15.2.2.1 Compared with exhaust system, positive ventilation affords better control of atmospheric conditions inside the factory building. Positive ventilation is useful where exhaust ventilation cannot be readily applied as in very large departments. In this system of ventilation, air is forced into the building by means of centrally located supply fans and is distributed 46

SP t 32 - 1986

FIG. 25

AN ARRANGEMENT FOR CRUSS VENTILATIONWITH FAN INSTALLED IN A CORNER OF THE ROOM the angle between the sides and axis of the duct should never exceed 30' and should preferably be not more than 15'. 15.2.3 Combined Systems - The combined systems having positive ventilation with supply of air through ducts and exhaust of air into return ducts have the advantage of providing better control of thermal environments and better distribution of air over the entire area of occupancy in particularly wider buildings. By supplying proper quantities of air in proportion to the heat load generated in respective areas at suitable velocities in the required areas through ductwork and by extracting the air in the return ducts in proportion to the supply air quantities and recirculating this air after properly mixing it with conditioned air ( evaporatively cooled or air-conditioned ), completely satisfactory environment is obtained. In certain departments where hot processes are carried on, advantage is taken of the natural upward movement of the air and floor-to-roof ventilation is obtained by a combination of forced under floor ventilation and roof extractors which are provided preferably over the heat-producing machines or processes. In a combined system it is preferable to provide slight excess of exhaust if there are adjoining occupied spaces and a slight excess of supply if there are no such spaces. Unit exhausters can also be used in combination with unit ventilators and located along outside walls. 15.3 Mechanical Roof Ventilators - Cowl type roof ventilators described earlier under ` Natural Ventilation ' can be equipped with fan barrel and motor thus permitting gravity operation or motorised high capacity, at will. Two types of roof ventilators are available: a) the vertical discharge or foundry-type, and b) the low-hood type. 15.3.1 In case of saw-toothed ( north-light) roofs, when these motor-driven roof ventilators are running to exhaust, the openings in the north-light within their area of influence should

through suitably located ducts. The fans are usually of centrifugal type or sometimes axial type with large capacity. Unit ventilators way be provided for individual roofs and may be placed against outside wall near the central line of the room. As mentioned earlier, the supply air can be cooled or conditioned, if desired, before it is passed into the plenum chamber and ducts ( see 16 and 17 ) and the installation equipped with systems of control that permits ventilating and air-conditioning effect to be varied, while the fans are operating continuously, to suit the requirements. The slight positive pressure set up within the building prevents inward leakage of cold or warm outside air. The volume of air admitted can be regulated and distributed in the desired manner through the ductwork. The air that can be set in motion by supply outlets is many times more than what is possible by exhaust. 15.2.2.2 Fresh air is drawn through SUCtion ducts or suction towers and is distributed into the building either by under-floor or overhead delivery ducts with outlets situated at intervals. Under-floor ductwork is generally of masonry construction and the outlets are provided in the floor at an interval of 4 to 6 m. In providing overhead ventilation, the air is brought from main ductwork to branch pipes or risers. Considerable advantage may be achieved by incorporating the ducts and risers into the building structure and by having interior surfaces off the ducts carefully finished to render them smooth and airtight and treated to prevent the possibility of duct being scoured from the walls of the ductwork by the passing air. In particularly hot areas, overhead ventilation may be provided by means of sheet metal ductwork either to improve the general comfort in the work place or to give local relief. 15.2.2.3 Ducts should be so designed and laid as to convey the air at suitable velocities with due regard to economy of materials and power. Ducts should be smooth and as straight as possible. Sharp bends and sudden enlargements and contractions should be avoided. For changing the direction or dimensions of a duct

SPr32-1986
by ` short-circulating `. In case of flatroofed or minitor-roofed buildings, combined positive and exhaust ventilation can be provided by roof ventilators, with alternate air inlet and exhaust adjacent to one another without the Exhaust fan will effect of ` short-circuiting `. exert very little influence beyond a velocity contour of about 15 m/min, which is just a short distance from the fan. The supply air, owing partly to forced ventilation and partly to negative pressure caused by ex!laust, will stream into the space below in a straight line until its momentum is spent or it runs into an obstruction. Although the supply and exhaust ventilators are adjacent, there will be no shortcircuiting of air between them if the throw of the supply air is sufhcient to reach the working level, but there will be, if the throw is much less than that. air, after getting mixed with the inside air, will be lowered to such an extend as to give adequate body cooling of workers and also remove possible difficulty caused by the rusting of equipment. 16.2 To deal with problems on evaporative cooling process or, for that matter, other airconditioning processes, an elementary knowledge of psychiometry ( hygrometry ) is required. Either relevant psychrometric tables on physical properties of moist air or psychrometric chart given in Fig. 26 may be referred to. The latter is more convenient to use as it shows graphically for a given barometric pressure the air properties, such as, dry bulb temperature, wet bulb temperature, specific humidity (moisture content) dew point, percent relative humidity, specific volume and total heat (speciand is particularly useful for fic enthalpy), representing processes in which air is cooled, heated, humidified, dehumidified or mixed with air from other sources. cooling process involving adiabatic saturation of air ( at almost constant enthalpy ) is represented by the outdoor wetbulb temperature line on the chart. Since in an evaporative cooling plant, leaving air dry-bulb temperature does not quite reach the entering, air wet-bulb temperature, that is, leaving air is somewhat short of saturation ( the degree of saturation depending on the number of water nozzles, their arrangement and their direction with respect to the direction of the air passing through the plant ), the saturation efficiency, or merely the efficiency, of the plant is defined in terms of the extent the leaving air dry-bulb temperature approaches the wet-bulb temperature, and is expressed as the ratio of the difference of the entering ( outdoor ) air dry-bulb temperature and the leaving air dry-bulb temrature to the difference of the entering air drybulb temperature at the wet-bulb temperature of the entering ( or leaving ) air. Or, saturation outdoor = outdoor efficiency DB -- leaving DB DB outdoor WB

16. EVAPORATIVE

COOLING

16.1 While discussing functions of ventilation, it was pointed out that to remove heat gained in a factory building and thus to bring down the temperature of air inside the building closer to that outside, large volumes ( quantities ) of outside air are required ( see 13.1 ). If the temperature of outside air is lowered before the air is discharged into the building, much less air will be needed and the cooled air could even be mixed with part of the inside air ( recirculated air ) before discharge. Air-cooling by mechanical refrigeration gives complete control of the environment ( see 17 ) and offers the greatest relief of course, but such a system is very expensive and may be difficult to justify, except in areas requiring controlled ambient conditions for product uniformity precision work or where the increased efficiency of the workers is reflected in a reasonable return on the investment of the system. In many situations, particularly in hot arid regions of the country where summers are hot and the humidity ( and therefore the wet-bulb temperature ) of air is low, evaporative cooling, using positive ventilation, has been found to be both economical and useful. Evaporative cooling may be employed effectively to lower the temperature of the supply air to near the wet-bulb temperature, which could take care of the indoor sensible heat loads and thus help in maintaining indoor conditions within the upper safe limits given in Table 11 or the temperature rise values at working level to within those indicated in Table 13. Through evaporative cooling, using only reasonable air quantities, the temperature inside the factory building may be lowered 5 to 10�C below the prevailing outside temperature depending on the outdoor wet-bulb temperature, the heat load and the number of air although humidity will changes per hour, be increased. But owing to large internal heat gain, the relative humidity of the discharged 48

16.3 The evaporative

16.3.1 This condition of air represents the air as it leaves the evaporative cooling plant. This air gets mixed with the air within the department and the final condition of the air after mixing will be represented by the quantity and quality of the air added to a given quantity of the air from the plant, that is, the proportion of the two by weight. If the sensible heat and latent heat loads of the department are known, the final condition will be determined by the line drawn from the point representing the air leaving the plant parallel to the line representing the sensible heat factor which is the ratio

SP : 32 - 1986
of the sensible heat to total heat (sensible heat plus latent heat ) load ( see Fig. 26 ). In case no latent heat is added in the department or the amount is insignificant, which happens when no process heat in the form of steam or other vapours is generated and the number of workers in the department is small and the workers are engaged in work of moderate intensity, the sensible heat factor is unity and the line is horizontal, that is, along the constant specific humidity line. 16.4 Evaporative cooling, properly applied, is the most practical means available to improve thermal environment in `hot' industries such as rolling mills, foundries, power houses. Central plant consisting of a `water spray chamber and a fan to supply outside air into the building through a distribution ductwork is far preferable to spray-head system within the building, which only humidifies the air but does not remove the heated air from the building. The system may be designed to accomplish cooling on the area basis or for spot cooling. For area cooling ducts should be designed to distribute the air in the lower 3 m of the space to assure supplying air where the workers are working. Since cooling {requirements vary from season to season and in fact from day to day, it is well to provide discharge grilles with some sort of adjustability. When the incoming temperature drops to a pomt ' as to create draughts, the workers can adjust the horizontal blades in the grilles so that the air is discharged above their heads and not directly on them. Area cooling lends itself well to applications where the workers move about within the space ( see 15.2.2.2 ). Spot cooling by overhead ducts yields a more efficient use of equipment when workers are relatively stationary and tend a group of machines. In these instances, cooled air can be brought in at levels even lower than 3 m. The selection of height would depend on the location of other equipment in the space. For best result the throw should be kept to the mimmum. Spot cooling is specially applicable in hot areas where man-cooling is needed.

industrial processes, evaporative air cooling may be used for maintaining sufficiently high humidity. Other examples are tobacco processing and cigar plants which impose high humidity requirements in various departments depending on the type of tobacco being used in the process.

17.AIR-CONDITIONING
17.1 When the manufacturing process requires a controlled temperature and humidity and these cannot be obtained by ventilation or evaporative cooling, air-conditioning may be resorted to. When refrigeration is employed to obtain desired temperature and humidity, it may be necessary to recirculate a part of the inside air after getting it mixed with fresh air to save on refrigeration. The fresh air should be drawn from areas where the air is not likely to be polluted or vitiated by any harmful dusts, fumes, gases, etc, given off into the working exhaust ducts or atmosphere from nearby chimney; and to make it free from any organic matter, the air should be efficiently filtered before it is supplied. 17~2 As far as possible, central air-conditioning system with ductwork may be employed, but where the requirements of air-conditioning are not high and are for a part of the building or processes, that part of the building may be partitioned and air-conditioned by means of window type or packaged type air-conditioning system with or without ductwork.

17.3.1 The size and number of air discharge outlets can be worked out from the quantity of air required to be forced into the building and the outlet velocities. This would depend on whether the air is to be delivered for general ventilation at a working level to replace the warm air rising from hot equipment, lights, occupants, etc, or whether the air is required for local area cooling or spot cooling with only a few small work areas or relatively few work stations. When the objective is to provide general ventilation at working level, supply air is delivered at about 3 m level at such discharge velocities as to cause secondary air movement and eddy currents and provide diffused air over the work stations. When the air is required for area cooling or spot cooling, the outlets should

SP : 32 - 1986 be kept close to the worker and, therefore, should be brought down to about 2 m level. Under-floor ventilation with outlets provided in the floor can be used in many cases provided air being discharged does not disturb the product or upset the performance of local exhaust hoods. For this purpose, the outlets have a pattern whereby the air is circulated in different directions at floor level. Sometimes, floor ventilators ( circulators ) of a particular shape are provided so as to give upward whirling movement and also to prevent direct blast into the work place, This type of ventilation is particularly useful when a few workers are employed who have to tend more than one machine or process and have to keep on moving from one place to another. 17.3.2 The level of air motion at the worker is important. For general ventilation, that is, when workers are engaged at fixed work stations in light activity, air movement should be kept low and should not exceed 60 m/min, but with high work levels and intermittent heat exposures, velocities as high as 5 to 10 m/s may be used. Care must be exercised in using very high air velocities to avoid the undesirable effects of air at high temperatures on body heat balance ( see 10.1.3 ). Further, the air should be delivered to the front and torso of the body. Impingement on the back of the head, neck and shoulders should be minimised. 17.3.3 The discharge velocity should be such as to obtain the desired velocity at the work station. If I',, is the velocity of air at the outlet having effective area A, the velocity Vx at distance X from the outlet is given by the eouation:

18.

MEASUREMENT

OF

VENTILATION

Total air quantity required to be discharged as seen from Example 6 has worked out to be 18 ms/s.

18.1 Efficiency of ventilation systems can be tested by ascertaining the rate of ventilation. The system should be run normally for certain hours and adjusted properly before it is tested. To measure the velocity of airflow, a properly calibrated vane-anemometer, velocity meter or It is necessary to make a pitot tube is used. traverse of the instrument over the crosssectional area of the inlet or outlet openings or ducts and obtain the average velocity from these results. The ventilation rate is the product of the average velocity and the net (free) area of ducts or openings.

52

SP : 32 - 1986
ventilation is by exhaust of air, the velocity of airflow at the fan outlets or at the air inlets on the opposite side can be measured by means of vane-anemometer, and the quantity of air passing is rapidly estimated. While taking measurements care should be taken to keep windows and other openings near the fans closed to eliminate the effects of cross currents or what is known as `shortcircuiting'. Similarly with the positive ventilation system, the air is impelled into the room so as to set up a slight positive pressure and the openings in the walls, etc, are therefore likely to serve as outlets only, unless they are large and numerous, when they can also serve as inlets of eddy or cross currents. In this case also, ventilation rate can probably be measured by the amount of air supplied by fans. When both positive ventilation or exhaust of air are functioning as in a combined system, the rate of ventilation should be reckoned as a higher of the two. 18.3 With natural ventilation also, direct measurement of ventilation rate is possible. The velocity of airflow through each individual ventilation opening can be measured by vane-anemometer, and the effective (free) area of each opening measured. Thus, the rate of airflow through each ,opening can be found out. It is usually found that the estimates of the total airflow through inlet openings and through outlet openings correspond remarkably well. For measuring ventilation rate in small rooms and offices, a tracer gas technique of measurement by the change in the is employed where concentration of some inert gas or vapour added into the atmosphere is measured and the rate of airflow worked out by a formula.

18.2 When

working area of the contaminants below their Threshold Limit Values (TLVs). The Threshold Limit Values refer to airborne concentratlons of contaminants and represent conditions of the environment under which it is believed that nearly all the workers may be repeatedly exposed, day after day (of an average 8 hours duration), without adverse effect. The current practice in this country regarding TLVs for contaminants is to refer to the values published by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists which are revised every year on the basis of research data or experience of its members.

19.1.1.1 When two or more contaminants are present in the air, their combined effect rather than that of either individually should be considered. In the absence of information to the contrary, the effect of the different contaminants should be considered as additive, that is, if sum of the following fraction,

CONTAMI19. VENTILATION FOR NANTS CONTROL 19.1 Local Exhaust Ventilation 19.1.1 When by reason of manufacturing
such as processes carried on, contaminants, dusts, fumes, gases and vapours are present in air within the work environment of a factory building to such an extent as are likely to be injurious or offensive to the workers, all measures must be taken to remove them. The best method is to provide an efficient local exhaust ventilation at the point at which the contaminants are released. Such point shall, as far as but if it is necessary to possible, be enclosed, have an access to the point to allow the processes to be carried on, the exhaust appliance should confine the contaminants as much as possible, and the openings should be located, possible, away from the natural wherever path of the contaminants travel so that the contaminants are carried away into the hood without their getting dispersed into the space where workers are working. The aim of providing the local exhaust ventilation is to reduce the concentration in the 53

19.1.2 When an exhaust appliance is such that the point at which the contaminants are released or generated is completely or partially enclosed, such as barrel filling, spray-painting booth, the volume of air required is calculated from the area of the openings and the capture velocity at the face of the openings to prevent outward escapement. In other cases, such as open tanks for degreasing, pickling and plating, and operations like welding, grinding, abrasive blasting, the volume of air required and the pattern of airflow in front of the exhaust appliance should be such that the capture velocities at the point of release or generation of the contaminants are sufficient to overcome air currents and capture the contaminants and convey them into the exhaust appliance. Recommended capture velocities for some of the manufacturing processes which are likely to give rise to the contaminants depending upon their condition of dispersion, are given in Table 18. These values are given as a guide and the actual velocities would depend on velocity of air flow and the distance through which the velocity acts. It would also depend on the air currents and draught at or near the exhaust. 19.1.3 The sizes of the ducts will be determined by the volume of air required and duct velocities necessary to convey the contaminants with minimum possible static resistance consistent with the economy of power and operational efficiency. are of low toxicity with a threshold limit value ( TLV ) above 100 ppm ( parts per million in air by volume ) such as vapours given off by organic solvents like carbon tetrachloride, and the quantity of contaminants generated is not high, or the contaminants are dispersed over a wide area, it is more economical to employ dilution ventilation to reduce the concentration of the contaminants in the working area below TLVs. It must be stated that this form of ventilation is not as satisfactory for control of air contaminants as local exhaust ventilation. What is achieved is that instead of appling exhaust at or near the source, ventilation is provided across the entire area of the contaminants generation. By this method the exhaust outlets and air supply inlets are so located that the air brought in from outside passes through the zone of contamination generation with the points at which the contaminants are released between the workers, and the exhaust outlets. The workers also should be advised not to stand too close to the zone where contaminants are released.

In these formulae X is a coefficient varying from 3 to 10 depending on the solvent in question, uniformity of air distribution, dilution of vapours in air, location of exhaust plant and its proximity to evolve vapours, and TLV is the threshold limit value of the solvent. 19.3

Make-Up Air

19.2 Dilution Ventilation 19.2.1 When the contaminents

19.3.1 When the volume of air exhausted either by local exhaust ventilation or by dilution ventilation is significant it will be necessary to bring in the work area sufficient make-up air at suitable points in relation to the exhaust points. This should be left either to natural infiltration of air through well-distributed windows or other suitable openings or brought about by positive ventilation, and, where necessary, the air should be filtered or treated. In no case makeup air should be brought in from outside areas which are contaminated by the exhaust ventilation, or dilution ventilation system. 19.3.2 While considering ventilation, due consideration should be given to the quality of outside air. The air brought in should not be dusty or contaminated by harmful contaminants, and if necessary, air should be filtered and other air treatment devices should be employed before the air is supplied by positive ventilation into the building.

A-l.1 Heat from People - The metabolic heat given off by the occupants is one of the sources of internal heat gain. A-l.2 Heat from Lighting - Heat from lighting apparatus is simply the aggregate rating of the tubes and bulbs installed, discounting those that will not be in use when solar heat gain is a major factor. Sometimes part of the ventilation air is extracted through special recessed lighting fittings. The convected heat from the lights will then be extracted with the air, and will not form part of the room heat load. The radiant heat load remaining will be about 80 percent of the rating for tungsten lamps, 60 percent for fluorescent. A-l.3 Heat from Electric Power - With very few exceptions the whole of the energy supplied to electrical apparatus will be dissipated as heat within the building. The maximum will be the full load rating of the appliance in kW, although allowance can be made for the dispersion factor when known. This factor is the ratio of the kilowatt-hours consumed in one hour to the kilowatt rating and takes account of both part-time and part-load working. Some times this factor can be obtained indirectly, for example, a machine shop may have statistics of the number of kWh of electricity consumed per shift or, better, the maximum half-hour kW demand. A-l.4 Heat from Electric Motors - In the case of an electric motor the usual rating is the output in kW, whereas what we require is the

A-l.5 Heat from Fuel - The combustion of fuel occurs in some part of the manufacturing process in most industrial plants. In many case it is a major factor, and general ventilation is necessary for the relief of heat stress, quite apart from local ventilation and other measures which are taken at the sources of heat. The potential heat load is easily obtained from the calorific value of the fuel and the rate at which it is used: kW = kJ/kg x kg/s However, a large part of this heat will not contribute to the environmental load. The deductions can be classified under three headings: a) Incomplete combustion - unburnt or partially burnt fuel passing up the flue.

b) Flue heat loss -

the heat - carried up the flue by hot gases comprising the products of combustion and the excess air,

c) Heat to stock - occurring when the material worked on (solid, liquid or gaseous) is heated and then passes, still hot, to other parts of the building. In important cases estimates for each of these items should be available as part of the manufacturing records or plans. More usually, perhaps, the margins of error in the direct calculation of the residual heat loss remaining within the building are too great. In such cases measurement of the actual air conditions on site will be more helpful. A-2. SOLAR HEAT

A-2.1 Heat from the Sun Solar heat reaches the earth at a fairly constant rate of I.36 kW/mz. I n passing through the atmosphere some of this heat will be absorbed or

SP : 32 - 1986
scattered into space. The proportion lost will be determined by the length of the part through the atmosphere and by the presence of clouds, dust, water vapour and ozone. Figure 27 gives representative values for a clear sky and various heights above sea level. The direct intensity, Id, varies with the altitude angle of the sun above the horizon. The effective intensity on any surface is further reduced by the inclination of the surface to the sun. In addition, diffuse radiation, If, reaches earth's surface after scattering dust and vertical walls receive tion from the ground. by atmospheric reflected radia-

A-2.2 Maximum Solar Heat Intensity However, our present aim is merely to estimate the ventilation rate required to limit the internal temperature in hot weather. For this purpose we need consider only that time of day and month of the year which will give the maximum solar heat :oad. This has been done in drawing up Tables 19 and 20 which can be used to estimate the maximum solar intensity on walls and roofs.
TABLE 19 MAXIMUM SOLAR INTENSITY VERTICAL WALLS

d) Take the intensity applied to the actual area of skylights, north lights, etc, from Table 20 according to their inclination to the horizontal towards or away from the sun when it faces wall (a). It should be noted that if the terrain is very bare and the air very dry, increased ground reflection and atmospheric clarity may increase tropical solar intensities by 20 percent. Conversely, industrial atmospheres may reduce intensities by 20 percent to 40 percent even on the sunniest days. Altitude corrections can be derived from Fig. 19, but for moderate heights an addition of 1 percent per 1CO m above sea level will suffice. The figures in the tables are for the time of year and day giving the highest intensity for each entry. The 24-hour average midsummer intensity averaged over walls equally exposed to all points of the compass is remarkably constant at about 0.08 kW/mz, with about 0.35 kW/ms on roofs. The tables may be used for the southern hemisphere by interchanging N and S. A-2.3 Calculation of Solar Heat Gain Having found the intensities of solar radiation falling on the faces of a building, the next step is to determine the total solar heat gain entering through windows, walls and roofs. This is, of course, proportional to the area of each surface, but reduced by a factor taking account of the heat excluded by reflection and external convection. Valves of this factor S for typical building features are given in Table 21.
